newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal's political leadership seen lacking vision.
newsitem.headline: Nepal's political leadership seen lacking vision.

text.p: Nepal's political leadership was responsible for instability in the Himalayan Kingdom and lacked vision to strengthen the fledgling democracy, analysts and business leaders said on Sunday.
They spoke as major political parties jostled to form the next government after the 17-month-old, centre-right coalition was voted out of power on Thursday.
"It is a total failure of the political leadership," Badri Bahadur Karki, a constitutional lawyer, told Reuters.
King Birendra on Friday set March 10 as the deadline for political parties to stake a claim to form the next government after Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba lost a vote of confidence and resigned.

Deuba was Nepal's fourth prime minister since the country embraced democracy in 1990. Nepal, which maintained self-imposed isolation until the middle of the century, is one of the world's 10 poorest nations with an annual average income of $200 a head.
"The political leadership who fought for democracy in Nepal did not have a well set agenda, both in the political and socio-economic field," said Devendra Raj Pandey, a leading political analyst.
Indecisive polls in November 1994 meant no party was able to win a majority in parliament and form a stable government. This led to confusion and instability, political analysts said.
"The hung parliament has to be hanged," said Karki, adding that fresh elections should be held. The next general poll is not scheduled until November 1999.
"The only positive factor is that all political parties appear to be wedded to the constitutional process," Pandey said.
But one politician, who declined to be identified, denied Nepal's political leadership was in disarray.
"It is not a crisis," he said.
Deuba's Nepali Congress party has said it was ready for a new coalition with the opposition Communist Unified Marxist-Leninist Party if they accepted its leadership.
Nepali Congress officials said the party's terms for potential partners included political stability and a code of conduct that would ensure the new government's smooth running.
Business leaders said Nepal's economy would suffer if political uncertainty remained unresolved.
"This is a very dangerous trend," said Banawarilal Mittal, who heads the Mittal Group of industries.
Political uncertainty was affecting investment decisions and threatening the continuation of liberal economic policies introduced in Nepal five years ago, he said.
"Investors need assurance that there is political stability," Mittal said.
The government was more pre-occupied with political issues and had gave little attention to economic policies, he added.
Price increases in recent months have also upset many Nepali citizens, analysts said.
Nepal's inflation rate was at 10.4 percent in mid-January compared with 9.4 percent six months ago in mid-July.
The country, with about 42 percent of its 21 million population below the poverty line, meets 60 percent of its cost of economic development from aid pledged by Western nations.
The International Monetary Fund recently urged the government to raise more local funds and step up privatization of some loss making state-owned units, officials said.
